extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of social/legal history of gambling; readers of literary/critical essays
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-historical account of gambling, lotteries, and the legal regimes governing them across countries and eras, together with social consequences and anecdotes. Useful for understanding historical practices, legal standards, and social critiques of gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancient gratuitous lotteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient Roman and medieval lotteries were often gratuitous—the tickets were given away, so if the people did not win anything they did not lose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the distinction between ancient 'lot' practices (e.g., Saturnalia distributions, gratuitous tickets under emperors) and modern paid-ticket lotteries; implies that harm arises primarily once money is paid for tickets.

rubrics_metrics.name: State lotteries as public revenue (origins in Italy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application of lotteries by paid tickets to the service of the state is said to have originated in Italy (Florence/Genoa) in the 16th century to raise revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how governments adopted lotteries as revenue tools—successful financially but later criticized for social harm; historical context for state sponsorship of gambling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old French lottery mechanics and house advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: The old French lottery used 90 numbers with drawings of five numbers; prizes (extrait, ambe, terne, quaterne) paid large multiples of the deposit, but the chances were greatly in favour of the state banker (e.g., extrait chances 18 to 15 against the player).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives concrete payout structures and shows mathematically how the 'bank' retained an advantage; exemplary detail for assessing fairness of a lottery scheme and how large advertised prizes can still favour the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary and English public lotteries history
rubrics_metrics.description: English lotteries (first cited 1569) later became parliamentary instruments (from 1709 to 1824) used to raise large sums for public projects; the last public lottery in Great Britain was drawn in 1826.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative of how lotteries were institutionalized and later suppressed—useful to evaluate the policy trade-off between public revenue and social costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurance of lottery numbers as a common fraud/overcharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Office-keepers insured numbers for the next day's drawing at premiums far above the just premium (e.g., charging 9s when the fair premium was 7s. 6d., and at later stages charging disproportionately higher sums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies an anti-pattern/abuse: secondary markets and 'insurance' schemes around lotteries often exploit players by charging excessive premiums and constitute flagrant impositions on the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lotteries induce widespread social harm (mendicity, crime, suicide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lotteries relaxed industry, fostered gambling across classes, filled pawnbrokers' shops, produced bankruptcies, thefts, forgeries, and increased suicides among the ruined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A normative/causal claim used throughout the chapter as a criterion for judging the wisdom of permitting lotteries; supports policy positions against lotteries on social-welfare grounds and cites contemporary observations and cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-drawn drawings create repeated temptation and insurance behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Until about 1800 lottery drawings could occupy some forty-two consecutive days, which kept gamblers engaged day after day and encouraged incremental betting/insurance as odds changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains a specific operational feature that magnified gambling addiction and financial loss; useful for evaluating lottery format risk and regulatory concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamburg model: near-full redistribution with minimal deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hamburg lottery redistributed all the money raised in prizes except for about 10% deducted for expenses and other charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a comparatively fairer administration of lotteries (from a payout perspective), but the author still views lotteries as pernicious despite fairer pooling; useful as a baseline for assessing relative fairness of different lottery systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private lotteries illegal in Great Britain and Ireland; penalties for foreign-lottery advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Private lotteries are illegal at common law in Great Britain and Ireland; advertisers of foreign lotteries also incur penalties. Attempts to evade the law (e.g., affixing a prize to every ticket) have been punished as fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes legal prohibitions and enforcement approaches in Britain: substantive prohibition of private lotteries and active suppression of evasions and advertising; cites specific statutes and 1870 enforcement on Christmas lotteries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art Unions tolerated but morally suspect
rubrics_metrics.description: Art Unions were tolerated under the eye of the law without express statutory exemption, but the author argues they tend to keep up the spirit of gambling and therefore ought not to be allowed even under the plea of promoting art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A policy/value judgment: tolerance by law does not equal moral acceptability; useful when weighing narrow exemptions against broader social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evasions and subterfuges around lottery laws (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evasions included selling photographs, attaching chances to struggling newspapers, or advertising raffles in satirical form—practical methods used to circumvent prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalogues concrete anti-patterns that lawmakers and enforcers should watch for when drafting/enforcing lottery restrictions; demonstrates how prohibition often provokes creative circumvention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancient Roman gaming law regime
rubrics_metrics.description: In ancient Rome all games of chance (except five relating to bodily vigour) were absolutely prohibited; losers could not be sued for moneys lost and could recover payments; third parties or municipal authorities could prosecute within long prescription periods; no surety for gambling payments was bound; betting on lawful games was restricted; persons whose houses hosted gambling lost civil redress; children and freedmen could recover losses against parents/patrons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed list of Roman legal rules demonstrating a stringent public-law response to gambling, including remedies for losers and penalties for keepers; useful as a historical model of prohibition with private-rights consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: French modern rule: no action for gambling debts except skill-based games
rubrics_metrics.description: By the present law of France judicial action is not allowed for gambling debts and wagers, except for games dependent on bodily skill (horse, foot, chariot races, etc.); courts may reject claims they deem excessive; monies paid generally cannot be recovered unless fraud is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also includes criminal sanctions for keepers/managers: fines (100–6000 francs), imprisonment (2–6 months), and possible deprivation of civil rights; gives both civil and criminal enforcement dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prussian gaming law principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Prussian Code: all games of chance are prohibited except when licensed; gaming debts are not actionable; wagers may be actionable when stakes are held by a third person; moneys lent for gambling cannot be sued for; keepers and gamblers punishable by fines or imprisonment; cheating obliges compensation; professed swindlers are punishable as thieves and may be banished; winnings from a drunken man must be returned if considerable, and a fine equal to the sum is payable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines civil non-enforceability of gambling contracts with criminal sanctions and special equitable protections (e.g., against taking advantage of intoxicated persons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Austrian prohibition-with-license model
rubrics_metrics.description: Austria: no right of action for winner or loser; all games of chance prohibited except when licensed by the state; cheating at play punished by imprisonment; allowing unlawful games in one's house subjects the party to heavy fines or imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes a licensing/forbearance model with strong criminal consequences and civil inaction for recovery of gambling losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian (Sardinian Code) rule: recovery only for skill or fraud/minority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sardinian Civil Code allows actions for moneys won at games of strength or skill when stakes are not excessive, but generally disallows recovery of moneys lost except on the ground of fraud or minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects the French-derived principle distinguishing skill-based contests from chance, and protects minors and fraud victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bavarian mixed-tolerance regime with proportional penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Bavaria: games of skill and mixed games are not forbidden; losers must pay and cannot recover provided games are honestly conducted and stakes not excessive relative to rank/fortune. In fraudulent or purely chance games the winner cannot claim and must repay; penalties escalate on repeated offenses (one-third, two-thirds, whole stake fines); keepers and those permitting gambling are punished; unlawful games may be legalized by authority but fraud/gross excess disables winners; immoral wagers are void; excessive wagers are reduced; betting on indifferent things is allowed; disparity of odds alone does not void a wager; cheating and professional swindling attract imprisonment, banishment, or hard labour (4–8 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex, pragmatic legal approach balancing toleration of skill-based play with sanctions for fraud and excess; provides many concrete enforcement mechanisms and equitable adjustments (e.g., reduction of excessive wagers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish principle: wagers lawful unless fraudulent/illegal/immoral
rubrics_metrics.description: Wagers in Spain are lawful provided they are not in themselves fraudulent, nor relate to anything illegal or immoral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A relatively permissive rule conditioned on legality and morality—useful as a comparative principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: English approach: selective prohibition and social-policy motives
rubrics_metrics.description: England forbade some forms of gaming under heavy penalties while tolerating others but discouraging them; legislative motives were sometimes policy-driven (e.g., 1541 act purportedly to preserve archery); the Gaming Acts (from Charles II's reign) aimed to check prevalent gambling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrays English law as pragmatic and historically shifting—some prohibitions motivated by military or social policy rather than purely moral objections.
